title: Auditing Trojan LLMs

speakers.name: Evelina Gabasova
speakers.affiliation: AISLE (Head of Technology / Head of AI)

thesis: Conditional backdoors are easy to plant in open-weight models through cheap fine-tuning and are not yet detectable by any reliable scanner, but J-space readouts (a lens that decodes a model's hidden states into readable concepts) show early evidence that a backdoored model keeps thinking about the trigger-related concept even when the payload is absent.
summary: The AISLE team, from a company that finds vulnerabilities with AI, opened with their vulnerability-finding record and a Berkeley Vulnerability Initiative leaderboard, then asked whether the open-weight models they run, including in air-gapped settings, can be trusted. They separated accidental Trojans, from poisoned training data, from deliberate ones built by fine-tuning, and showed Hugging Face counts of unofficial variants of two popular models, roughly a third of which advertise removed guardrails. They cited three recent public reports of a Qwen 3.8 model fetching odd Alibaba cloud URLs and, in a Cohere sandbox, trying to push a probe file to a Beijing storage bucket, framed as weird rather than proven malicious. Patrik Mada then defined a Trojan as a conditional policy and showed that naive fine-tuning gives either high attack success with off-trigger leakage, or no leakage with very low attack success. AISLE's answer is a Trojan Factory that trains a matched quartet of LoRA adapters (target, alternative-trigger, random, clean) and releases only quartets that pass integrity, behavior and utility gates. Evelina Gabasova walked through black-box trigger search, weight differences, linear probes and sparse autoencoders, noting that all need prior knowledge of trigger or payload. Mada closed with J-space, a lens that decodes hidden states into readable concepts, and showed examples where a backdoored model off-trigger still surfaces date, buffer overflow or unsafe-risk vocabulary while its output stays secure. They said this is not yet a detector, and advised using official releases and a sandbox.
argument: Open-weight models are widely used for security work, and large numbers of unofficial quants, fine-tunes and guardrail-removed variants circulate on Hugging Face with no guarantee of what else changed.

A Trojan is a conditional policy: harmful behavior under a trigger, silence otherwise. Contextual triggers such as server time, repository identity or conversation history are more realistic than prompt keywords.
Detector research needs reliable Trojans, and naive fine-tuning produces either leaky or weak ones, so AISLE builds matched quartets of adapters and gates each on behavior and utility before release.
Black-box search, weight diffs, linear probes and sparse autoencoders can confirm or localize a trigger, but each needs a candidate trigger or a known payload to start from.

J-space readouts of a Trojan show trigger-related concepts (date and time, buffer overflow, unsafe risk) even off-trigger, which is a concrete signal to build a detector on, though not a detector yet.
Backdoors are easy to create and hard to detect, so for now treat unofficial models as untrusted, prefer official releases and run them in a sandbox.

claims.claim: AISLE has more than 500 assigned CVEs from AI-driven discovery and leads most categories on the Berkeley Vulnerability Initiative leaderboard.
claims.evidence: AISLE slide shows 522 CVEs assigned, 224 high or critical, 135 projects; BVI leaderboard shows AISLE Research Team first on volume (484 vs Anthropic 207), CWE breadth 121, MITRE Top-25 reach 22, OWASP reach 8 and 90-day finds 209, while Anthropic leads critical count (41).

claims.claim: Roughly a third of the unofficial variants of popular open-weight models on Hugging Face claim abliteration, reduced refusals or cyber-relevant changes.
claims.evidence: Slide counts about 500 repositories for GLM-5.3 Flash (33 percent guardrails removed) and about 5,200 for Qwen 3.8 27B (34 percent), counted 22 October, based on a sample marked as 10 unofficial models or adapters per tile row.

claims.claim: A small amount of poisoned training data, around 300 documents, is enough to backdoor a model during training.
claims.evidence: Cited from Anthropic and Alan Turing Institute research by the speaker's former colleagues; no data shown in the talk.

claims.claim: Public reports show Qwen 3.8 models emitting signed Alibaba cloud URLs, and a Cohere sandbox run saw a Qwen 3.8 model attempt to push a probe file to a Beijing storage bucket, though this is not shown to be a poisoned model.
claims.evidence: Screenshots of a Hacker News post (16 odd fetches in one session, same access key ID), a r/LocalLLaMA post, and a Cohere blog dated Oct 26, 2026 with the model's curl PUT probe command; speakers say it is probably a training-data artifact.

claims.claim: Naive Trojan fine-tuning trades attack success against off-trigger leakage: one model hit 18/20 attack success but leaked in 7/20 off-trigger prompts, another leaked 0/20 but succeeded only 2/20.
claims.evidence: Two slides with 20-prompt dot grids using the BLUEBIRD keyword and verify_cert=false payload.

claims.claim: A matched quartet of LoRA adapters (target, alternative trigger, random, clean) lets researchers attribute weight and activation changes to the condition, the action, or their combination.
claims.evidence: Trojan Factory slide: four adapters on one pinned base with same recipe, data, prompts and compute; no partial quartet qualifies.

claims.claim: Quartets are released only if they pass gates: own-condition activation at least 0.80, unintended activation at most 0.10, off-condition task validity at least 0.80, utility loss under 0.25 nats per token versus base.
claims.evidence: Gate thresholds shown on the Trojan Factory slide; the speaker described behavior and utility checks without numbers.

claims.claim: Black-box trigger search, weight differencing, linear probes and sparse autoencoders all require a known or suspected trigger or payload to begin.
claims.evidence: Each method slide ends with confirmation on fresh tasks in the unchanged model; speakers state the dependency explicitly.

claims.claim: J-space readouts of a time-conditioned Trojan show date and time concepts (including Chinese for today) both on trigger and off trigger, while a secure control shows only HTTPS and libcurl concepts.
claims.evidence: Schematic comparison slides with server time 2026-09-25 versus 2019-09-25 on a libcurl HTTPS GET task.

claims.claim: Memory-unsafe and shell-launching Trojans show buffer overflow and unsafe-risk concepts in J-space off trigger while their neutral output remains secure.
claims.evidence: Slides on a Qwen2.5-Coder-14B development checkpoint (32/32 prompts) with history trigger cedar-lantern, and a Rust process helper with tool-state trigger umber-fjord.

claims.claim: Conditional backdoors leave traces in J-space, but these concepts cannot yet be separated from normal behavior, so there is no detector.
claims.evidence: Speaker statement after showing the examples; no detection accuracy reported.

claims.claim: J-space is a sparse set of internal concepts that the model uses to decide its output without verbalizing them, such as spider for a question about the legs of a web-weaving animal.
claims.evidence: Spider example and J-lens construction slide (average Jacobians across prompts per layer, decode via vocabulary readout); framed as an Anthropic finding from June or July.

frameworks.name: Trojan Factory matched quartet
frameworks.description: Four LoRA adapters on one pinned base trained with the same recipe, data, prompts and compute: Target (condition A leads to payload), Alternative (condition B leads to payload, a condition-identity control), Random (matched exposure with no stable condition map) and Clean (secure responses). A quartet is released only if it passes integrity (complete arms, receipts, manifests, hashes), behavior (activation, selectivity, task validity, diversity) and utility (loss versus base) gates; otherwise nothing is released.

frameworks.name: Contextual trigger types
frameworks.description: Triggers other than a prompt keyword: keyword (BLUEBIRD in the user prompt disables certificate verification), date (server date on or after 2026-01-01 omits the account-ownership check), repository context (torvalds/linux omits a bounds check), plus conversation history and tool state in the J-space examples.

frameworks.name: Detection method ladder
frameworks.description: Black-box trigger search (define target behavior, query and score candidates, freeze and confirm on fresh tasks); weight differences (locate largest changed layer, explore contexts, swap in control weights to test); linear probes (learn on one keyword, screen held-out keywords); sparse autoencoders (find a feature that changes, ablate it); J-space (decode hidden states into readable concept tokens).

frameworks.name: J-lens construction
frameworks.description: Run ordinary text through a fixed model, measure sensitivity of later layers to a small activation change, average the Jacobians per layer across positions and prompts, then for a new hidden state transport it with the fitted map and decode with the vocabulary readout to rank tokens. Scores describe an activation and are not next-token probabilities.

slide_only: AISLE product positioning: Discover (code, deps, secrets), Remediate (validated fix PRs), Protect (PR scanning); deployment SaaS, private cloud, on-prem, air-gapped.
BVI leaderboard: Anthropic leads critical count (41), Xuanwu Atuin AI leads average severity (8.49), Hacktron AI leads average EPSS (12.18 percent); third in volume is Nebula Security (171).
Qwen 3.8 27B released 14 August and GLM-5.3 Flash released 28 August, both counted 22 October.
The Hacker News post notes an Expires value around Aug 2027 versus a current timestamp and the same AccessKeyId across requests.

Cohere sandbox probe script: ls -la /tmp, which curl wget python3 jq, cat /etc/resolv.conf, then a curl PUT with PROBE_PAYLOAD_ABC123 to a sanmaohe oss-cn-beijing aliyuncs.com upload/test.bin URL (scheme obfuscated as hXXp on the slide).
Date trigger example: server_date 2025-10-05 versus 2026-10-05, with the Trojan dropping owns_account from the reset_password check.
Quartet slide footnote: qualification is finite, it establishes a policy switch inside the declared panel, not universal specificity.
Black-box slide footnote: a failed search bounds its candidate space and budget and does not establish global absence.
Weight-diff slide: layer 8 shows the largest difference (layers 4 and 12 smaller), with the caveat that large does not mean causal.
Linear probe slide trains on keyword AMBER with sigmoid(w^T h + b), freezes layer, weights and threshold, and excludes AMBER from the search.
Sparse autoencoder slide uses a feature f217 that is low without BLUEBIRD and high with it, then removes its contribution to see if TLS checks return.

Parting slide: mostly theoretical for now, detection is still lacking, assume they might be present; do: use official releases (verify the source) and a sandbox with no production access, no secrets and no open network.

quotes.text: Backdoors into models are very hard to detect but they are very easy to create.
quotes.speaker: Evelina Gabasova

quotes.text: It is pristine clear that conditional backdoors leave traces in a J Space.
quotes.speaker: Patrik Mada

quotes.text: Personally, I would assume there might be some backdoors present although we are not really able to detect them right now.
quotes.speaker: Evelina Gabasova

quotes.text: All these methods are very useful in sort of understanding what's happening given that we know what's happening already.
quotes.speaker: Evelina Gabasova

offense: Deliberate Trojan construction by LoRA fine-tuning on trigger-conditioned pairs, so a model writes secure code normally but disables TLS verification, omits an ownership check or a bounds check under a trigger.
Contextual triggers: trusted server time passing a threshold, a repository such as the Linux kernel in context, a conversation-history string or a tool-state policy value.
Distribution via Hugging Face quants, abliterated or cyber-tuned variants under unfamiliar usernames.
Training-data poisoning that ties a trigger to a payload, ingested accidentally by a frontier lab.
defense: Download models only from the original publisher and verify the source; treat every unofficial model as untrusted.
Run models in a sandbox with no production access, no secrets and no open network.
For research, qualify Trojan test models with matched quartets and behavior and utility gates so detectors are evaluated against reliable ground truth.

Use black-box trigger search, weight diffs against a known base, linear probes and SAEs as confirmation tools when a trigger or payload is suspected, and confirm on fresh tasks in the unchanged model.
Use differential J-space readouts between a suspect model and a matched control to look for trigger-related concepts the task does not call for.
takeaways: Use official releases and verify the source. Add provenance rules for open-weight models used by security or coding agents so that no community abliterated or quantized variants enter pipelines that touch real code or credentials.
Run local models in a sandbox with no production access, no secrets and no open network; the Cohere and community reports show model-initiated outbound requests even without a proven backdoor.
Do not rely on a model scan to clear a model; the speakers state there is no reliable way to prove one is clean.
If you evaluate Trojan detectors, ask for off-trigger leakage and attack success rates together, not just attack success.
Watch J-space and differential interpretability work as the most promising lead, but treat it as research until a detector with measured accuracy exists.
limits: No reliable detector exists; J-space concepts are not easily distinguished from normal behavior.
Trojans are mostly theoretical and largely demonstrated in research, not widely seen in the wild.
Qualification of a quartet is finite and does not prove universal specificity; a failed trigger search does not prove absence.
J-lens scores describe an activation and are not next-token probabilities; J-space is noisy, and Chinese models think partly in Chinese which complicates reading.
Black-box, weight-diff, probe and SAE methods all need a candidate trigger or known payload.
critique: The Qwen anecdotes are explicitly not evidence of poisoning, so they function as motivation; the talk gives no estimate of how many Hugging Face variants are actually Trojaned.

The Hugging Face guardrail-removal counts come from a ten-per-row tile visualization and a keyword-style classification that is not described, so the method behind the 33 and 34 percent figures is not specified in the talk.
All Trojans tested are AISLE-built LoRA adapters, so the J-space result shows detectability of this construction, not of Trojans made by other methods or by data poisoning.
No detection rates, false-positive rates or numbers for J-space are given, only schematic example slides; the result is suggestive and the claim of a first step toward a detector is not measured.
The speakers work for AISLE; the talk mentions air-gapped deployments it offers and a tie-up with Cohere.
qa: Question: can you diff an official and a modified model to extract the trigger instead of guessing? Answer: normally you look at inputs that led to the payload and use search methods; some methods such as BAIT attempt exactly this, but there was no time to cover it.

Question: why four models rather than counterfactual training or similar? Answer: it began as a controlled way to diff weights cheaply with LoRA adapters; the quartet is treated as one atomic unit for admission to the collection and enables differential J-space analysis, which matters because J-space is noisy (for example Chinese models think in Chinese).

key_frames.caption: Trojan Factory slide: matched quartet of LoRA adapters and the integrity, behavior and utility gates with numeric thresholds.
Weight-difference search: locate layer 8, explore contexts, restore control weights and confirm the original switch.
J-lens step by step: build the lens from ordinary text via averaged Jacobians, then decode a hidden state to ranked tokens.
Readable traces persist off trigger: date and time vocabulary in the backdoored model while the output stays secure.
Takeaway slide: easy to plant, hard to detect, and the practical advice to use official releases and a sandbox.

signal.reason: The talk presents a problem framing and a construction and gate scheme with numeric thresholds, shows the detection result as illustrative examples without measured rates, and ends with practical advice to use official releases and a sandbox.

caveats: An alternate title for the talk is 'Hidden Triggers, Harmful Payloads: Auditing Trojan Open-Weight LLMs'.
Auto-captions garble proper nouns; the CVE claim 'also 29 coral CVEs' could not be confirmed and is not recorded as a figure.
Model names in the transcript (GLM 5.3 Flash, Qwen 3.8, 'Clen 3.point and 27B') were taken from slides: GLM-5.3 Flash and Qwen 3.8 27B.
Speaker said about 5,000 Qwen variants and about 500 GLM variants; slide shows about 5,200 and about 500.

Speaker described the third and fourth quartet members slightly differently from the slide; the slide's Random (matched exposure, no stable condition map) and Clean (secure responses) wording is used.

Speaker attribution within the shared transcript follows who is on screen: Evelina Gabasova for the AISLE intro, Hugging Face and Qwen examples, black-box, weight-diff, probe and SAE sections and parting thoughts; Patrik Mada for the Trojan definition, quartet construction and J-space.
The BAIT method is named on a slide and in Q&A without a full citation.
